sections.title: Featured Case Study: WooCommerce Rebuild, Start to Finish

inline: The WooCommerce skincare rebuild is the clearest example of how we approach a project. It shows the scope, the numbers, and the process, in the format you should expect from any developer you evaluate.

The client had a WooCommerce store running 27 plugins, with a mobile load time over six seconds and a checkout completion rate well below the category benchmark. The store handled product variations poorly, and the plugin stack was causing periodic conflicts at checkout.

items: Ran a full plugin audit and removed or replaced 11 plugins.
Rebuilt the theme in a child theme to keep customizations update-safe.
Optimized images, implemented critical CSS, and set up a caching layer.
Simplified checkout logic and removed an unnecessary app that added two seconds to the flow.
Added automated backups, security hardening, and a maintenance schedule.
Mobile load time improved from 6.1s to 1.9s.
Checkout completion up 21% over the first 90 days.
No critical bugs post-launch; no plugin conflicts in the first six months.
Ongoing maintenance reduced from roughly 6 hours per month to under 2.

inline: will help you spot the warning signs.
The pattern in positive reviews is almost always the same. Across 37 reviews, these are the themes clients mention most often.

Clients consistently mention that they knew where the project stood at every stage, and that questions were answered the same day. Communication is the single most common theme in positive reviews, and its absence is the most common theme in negative ones.

Projects that ran well were scoped into clear milestones with defined deliverables. Clients mention this specifically because it is what let them plan around the launch and avoid the last-minute scramble.
A recurring theme is that the launch did not reveal a long list of new costs or bugs. This is what a written scope and a proper QA process produce.
Clients who stay with us for maintenance mention that the ongoing support is genuinely proactive, not just reactive fixes after something breaks.

Our projects range from first ecommerce stores to multi-store replatforms. The common thread is that the client knows what they need and wants a developer who can deliver it without a lot of hand-holding.

sections.title: How to Verify Any Developer's Portfolio (Including Ours)

inline: This section is here because we believe the same standard should apply to every developer you evaluate, not just us. The checks below are what we would want a client to run on our portfolio.

blocks.text: Open the live store on mobile

inline: Do not rely on screenshots. Open each live store on your phone and go through the checkout. If the store is slow, broken, or clearly a stock demo, that tells you everything you need to know.
Ask the developer for their specific role on each project. On larger builds, they may have built one section rather than the whole store. That is fine if they tell you.
A good developer will cite specific numbers: load time before and after, conversion change, or order volume. A weak answer is a screenshot without a metric.
Any developer with a healthy portfolio can produce two references. If they cannot, that is a red flag. For the full checklist, see

t: the 12 vetting questions

inline: in our pillar guide.

blocks.text: Check the case study matches the portfolio

inline: If a developer cites a portfolio store but cannot produce a case study, timeline, or client reference for it, treat the portfolio claim with skepticism. For warning signs to watch for, see

t: common red flags when hiring an ecommerce developer
